title: Twelve guesses at Rome
hook: Astronomers and mapmakers spent centuries on one short distance. How close did they get?

knows: latitude and longitude locate a place
doesNotKnow: that the errors ran almost all one way and were huge even for a short, well-travelled distance, because longitude needed time

misconception: Old estimates scattered around the truth, so their average was about right.
objective: The learner can say that all twelve pre-1644 estimates of the Toledo-Rome longitude difference put Rome too far east (only one within 2 degrees; the middle one about 780 km too far), and that longitude was hard because it needs a difference in local time.

claims.text: Twelve astronomers and mapmakers before 1644 estimated the longitude difference from Toledo to Rome; the stage draws their twelve values and years.
claims.source: history-data.mjs: langren, Langren1644.csv, columns Name, Year, Longitude (van Langren 1644, digitised by Friendly et al. 2010). The 12 rows are copied into Demo.tsx unrounded; check section 6 of company/domains/briefs/checks/history-cycle1-check.mjs.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Re-derived in my own node script from the pinned file (history-data.mjs pins all hold; sha256 re-checked) and compared with the copied array in Demo.tsx (identical). Langren1644.csv has 12 rows; all 12 (Name, Year, Longitude) are in Demo.tsx DATA unchanged; years 150-1610. HistData Langren1644 doc (opened from raw.githubusercontent.com) describes them as 'determinations of the distance in longitude between Toledo and Rome, from the 1644 graph', Source column Astron 7 / Map 5, so 'astronomers and mapmakers' is right. | FC pass 43 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): correction to the pass-39 note above, status unchanged: the Source column is Map 2 / Astron 10 (pinned CSV and CRAN HistData 1.1.1 Langren1644.RData), not Astron 7 / Map 5 (that is the Gap column). 'Astronomers and mapmakers' still holds.

claims.text: Toledo to Rome is 16.5 degrees of longitude.
claims.source: HistData Langren1644 documentation (opened by cm-history): Toledo 39.86 N, 4.03 W; Rome 41.89 N, 12.5 E; 12.5 - (-4.03) = 16.53. history-cycle1-check.mjs section 6, '6 true distance'.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HistData Langren1644 doc opened: 'toledo <- c(39.86, -4.03); rome <- c(41.89, 12.5)'; 12.5 + 4.03 = 16.53, shown as 16.5. Demo.tsx computes TRUE from the same constants.

claims.text: Only 1 of 12 came within 2 degrees (G. Jansonius, 1605: 17.7), and every one put Rome too far east: the estimates ran from 17.7 to 30.1 degrees.
claims.source: Computed in Demo.tsx from the 12 rows (|lon - 16.53| <= 2; min, max; count lon > 16.53); same as history-cycle1-check.mjs section 6 ('6 within 2 degrees', '6 all too far east').
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Re-derived in my own node script from the pinned file (history-data.mjs pins all hold; sha256 re-checked) and compared with the copied array in Demo.tsx (identical). |lon - 16.53| <= 2: only G. Jansonius 1605, 17.736; all 12 > 16.53; min 17.736, max 30.128 (shown 17.7, 30.1). Demo.tsx WITHIN, EAST, LO, HI use the same rules.

claims.text: The middle estimate was 25.8 degrees, 9.3 degrees too far, about 780 km.
claims.source: Median of 12 = mean of the 6th and 7th sorted values (25.617, 26) = 25.81; 25.81 - 16.53 = 9.28 degrees x 111.32 x cos(40.875 deg) = 84.2 km per degree = 781 km, rounded to the nearest 10 = 780. Computed in Demo.tsx; history-cycle1-check.mjs section 6 '6 middle estimate in km'. The stage's 500 km scale bar uses the same km per degree.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Median (25.617 + 26) / 2 = 25.8085; minus 16.53 = 9.2785 degrees; 111.32 x cos(40.875 deg) = 84.173 km/degree; 781.0 km, rounded to tens = 780. Demo.tsx MEDIAN, KM_PER_DEG, MEDIAN_KM are the same formulas.

claims.text: Sorted by year, the estimates show no steady improvement: the earliest (150) is 27.8 and the latest (1610) is 28.2.
claims.source: Rows sorted by the Year column: C. Ptolomeus 150, 27.787; A. Argelius 1610, 28.17. history-cycle1-check.mjs section 6 '6 no steady improvement by year'.
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Sorted by Year: C. Ptolomeus 150, 27.787 (27.8); A. Argelius 1610, 28.17 (28.2). Demo.tsx BY_YEAR.

claims.text: Latitude can be read from the Sun or a star, but longitude needs the difference in local time between two places (one hour = 15 degrees).
claims.source: Convention: 360 degrees / 24 hours = 15 degrees per hour (geography:sun-time-from-longitude). Brief 6 claim (4).
claims.note: FC pass 39 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Derivation checked: local solar time changes by 360/24 = 15 degrees of longitude per hour of the Earth's turn, so a longitude difference is a local-time difference; latitude follows from the altitude of the Sun or the pole star. Geometry, not a cited fact.

claims.text: ... which nobody could then measure well.

recall.question: Two clocks: one set to noon where you are, one to noon at your home port. They differ by 2 hours. How far east or west are you?
recall.why: The Earth turns 15 degrees an hour, so a 2-hour difference in local time is 30 degrees of longitude. Without a way to compare times, longitude could not be measured well.
